issues.legal_issue: A special statutory proceeding for eviction that provides a complete procedure does not require a separate notice terminating the tenancy under the general property law.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction through a statutory rent-control proceeding after the tenant defaulted on rent.
The statute provided a special procedure for eviction and contained the requirements for that procedure.

The landlord had sent a notice terminating the tenancy, but the court proceeded on the basis that the statutory eviction process did not require compliance with the general property-law notice provision.
issues.conclusion: The special statutory eviction proceeding did not require a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act; the High Court correctly applied that principle, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, where the statute provides a complete special procedure for eviction, a separate notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is unnecessary. The Court relied on the principle applied in Ulligamma v. S. Mohan Rao, and on Raval & Co. v. K. C. Ramachandran and Shri Hem Chand v. Shrimati Sham Devi. It distinguished Mangilal v. Sugan Chand Rathi, which concerned an ordinary civil suit and a statutory provision that merely barred such suits subject to exceptions.

predicates.special_statutory_eviction_proceeding: The party seeking eviction pursued a special statutory proceeding for eviction of a tenant.
predicates.complete_statutory_eviction_process: The statutory process provided the requirements for obtaining eviction through that proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party seeks eviction through a special statutory proceeding and that process supplies the requirements for eviction, a separate tenancy-termination notice is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A postman need not invariably be produced to establish service of a registered letter returned with an endorsement that it was refused.
material_facts: A registered notice sent to the tenant was returned with an endorsement that the tenant had refused to accept it.
The tenant denied receiving the notice, and the postman who attempted delivery was not produced.
The Court explained that a recipient’s denial may be found incorrect from the recipient’s admissions or conduct, and that the presumption arising from a refusal endorsement is rebuttable.
issues.conclusion: It is not always necessary to produce the postman; a denial of service may be found incorrect from the recipient’s own admissions or conduct. The Court did not further determine whether the notice in this case had been served, because it upheld the decision on the separate issue concerning the statutory eviction process.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 114 of the Evidence Act, a registered letter returned with an endorsement of refusal may support a rebuttable presumption that it was received and refused in the ordinary course of business. Nirmalabala Debi v. Provat Kumar Basa correctly stated that the endorsement may support that presumption without examining the postman; Meghji Kanji Patel v. Kundanmal Chamanlal was consistent because the presumption there had been rebutted by the recipient’s sworn evidence. A denial may be disproved through the recipient’s admissions or conduct, so postman testimony is not invariably necessary.

predicates.registered_notice_service_dispute: A party disputes whether a registered notice was served on its intended recipient.
predicates.refusal_endorsement: The registered notice was returned with an endorsement that the recipient refused to accept it.
predicates.recipient_admissions_or_conduct_indicate: The recipient’s own admissions or conduct indicate that the recipient knew of or refused the notice.

issues.definition: When service of a registered notice is disputed, the notice bears a refusal endorsement, and the recipient’s admissions or conduct indicate knowledge or refusal, the postman’s testimony is not invariably required.
